newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Recent cocoa rally may be premature-analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Recent cocoa rally may be premature-analysts.

text.p: The recent run-up in world cocoa prices may be premature based on the market's fundamental outlook, despite a supportive technical picture, industry analysts said.

"The technical situation makes it hard to be caught up in the fundamentals," said Dean Witter analyst Corey Bell. "But there is no reason for it to continue to rally because there is not a concrete fundamental situation supporting the rally.
"Technically, there may be still room on the upside," he added. "But I'd like to see something fundamental underpinning it and it is too early to confirm talk of a decline in production."

On Wednesday, CSCE cocoa futures tumbled ahead of midday on local selling and light speculative profit-taking, but scale-down trade buying and some short-covering prevented further losses, dealers said.
Benchmark CSCE September cocoa fell $28 a tonne as of 1122 EDT, to $1,684, after sinking to a low of $1,675.
In London, LIFFE cocoa futures posted moderate losses on light profit-taking, with the active September delivery month down 10 stg, to 1,136 stg.
Analysts noted today's downturn was relatively modest in view of cocoa's recent rally.
Since the start of June, CSCE cocoa futures have shot-up 15 percent to their highest levels in nine years, while London cocoa futures ran up to one-year highs on Tuesday.
The rally has been fueled by keen speculative buying amid bullish technicals and concerns a developing El Nino weather pattern could adversely affect the 1997/98 cocoa harvest.
"Two things have supported this rally," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast.

"Bullish sentiment as been collecting since last winter when technicians looked at charts and said: 'This thing could go to $2,000.' After it went over $1,543, it thrilled technicians and at the same time the El Nino effect was talked about in this market."
Many meterologists predict El Nino, a cyclical, warm current in the Pacific Ocean than has been linked in the past to drought in many cocoa-growing regions, is making a comeback this year.
But Prendergast and other analysts warned that it is still very early to gauge the impact of El Nino on next year's harvest.

"El Nino is certainly in play, but it is at the early stages and it is not clear yet what effects it will have on crops," Prendergast said. "El Nino is strongly marked with the label of 'buy the rumor, sell the fact.' We just don't know what's out there."

Fears have emerged that recent dry weather in Indonesia -- the world's third-largest producer of cocoa -- are related to the weather phenomenon, and concerns have grown that top-producer Ivory Coast could also be impacted.

Some preliminary forecasts from the Ivory Coast have pointed to a reduced cocoa harvest in 1997/98, but Ivorian weather analysts have said recently that heavy rainfall during June has boosted prospects for the 1997/98 main cocoa crop.
Additionally, some analysts said the market may be ahead of itself in view of the current abundent supply of cocoa.
"As far as the stock situation is concerned, there is plenty of cocoa available," noted Dean Witter's Bell.
Both Bell and Prendergast estimated the fair price for cocoa given the current fundamental picture would be near the $1,600 a tonne level.

"The $1,600 area would be a fair valus and cash values suggest that," Bell said. "But the market's still positive technically and we may not see anything negative fundamentally until the Fall when we get a better idea what the crop will look like." ((Patricia Avidan, New York Commodity Desk, +1 212 859 1640))
